subject: physics
question_text: What are the limitations (drawbacks) of the first law of thermodynamics?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 (Thermodynamics) Short Answer Question 4 (printed p.127). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the first law conserves energy but does not fix the direction of a process (it does not forbid heat flowing from a colder to a hotter body), does not say whether an energy-conserving process is physically possible, and sets no limit on the efficiency of converting heat into work; the second law (Clausius and Kelvin–Planck statements) supplies all three.

steps.label: No direction of the process
lines: The first law only balances energy;
it does not say WHICH WAY a process
actually goes.
It permits heat to flow from a
colder body to a hotter one, since
energy would still balance — but
this never happens in nature.
steps.margin_note: Give the cold-to-hot example — it is the standard illustration of this drawback.
steps.why: This is the textbook example that shows the gap directly: the first law has nothing to say against a process everyone knows is impossible.
common_mistakes: Saying the first law is wrong. It is correct; it is only silent on direction.
Giving no example — the cold-to-hot case is what makes the drawback concrete.
steps.memory_tip: Energy balances both ways; only the second law says which way is real.

steps.label: No statement on whether a process is possible
lines: The first law says only that
energy is conserved in a process.
It does not say whether a process
consistent with that balance can
actually happen at all.
Deciding what is possible needs a
separate law.
steps.margin_note: This is a separate point from direction — say it as its own sentence, not folded into the first drawback.
steps.why: A process can conserve energy on paper and still be physically impossible — the first law offers no way to tell the two apart.
common_mistakes: Merging this with the direction drawback. They are two separate gaps: WHICH WAY, and WHETHER AT ALL.
Saying the first law predicts outcomes. It only checks a balance; it does not predict.
steps.memory_tip: Conserved on paper is not the same as possible in practice.

steps.label: No limit on efficiency
lines: The first law sets no limit on how
much of a given heat can be turned
into work.
It would allow an engine that
converts ALL the heat it takes in
completely into work, with none
rejected — which is never seen in
practice.
steps.margin_note: This is the drawback the second law's Kelvin–Planck statement directly closes.
steps.why: An engine at 100% efficiency conserves energy exactly as well as a real one; only a separate law about heat and work sets the actual ceiling.
common_mistakes: Saying the first law limits efficiency to less than 100%. It sets NO limit at all — that is the drawback.
Confusing this with the direction drawback — this one is about work, not about which way heat flows.
steps.memory_tip: The first law has no ceiling on efficiency; the second law puts one there.

steps.label: What the second law adds
steps.mark_note: The second law supplies all three
lines: Direction, possibility and the
efficiency limit are three separate
gaps the first law leaves open.

lines.text: The second law supplies all three.

steps.margin_note: Name all three gaps together in this closing line — direction, possibility, efficiency limit.
steps.why: The question asks for the drawbacks of the first law, and naming what fixes them is what shows the answer is complete, not just a list.
common_mistakes: Listing only one or two of the three gaps in the closing line and leaving the count incomplete.
Explaining what the second law says in full — the question only asks what the first law fails to do, not the second law's own statements.
steps.memory_tip: Three gaps, one law that closes them: direction, possibility, efficiency limit.

insider_note: Three separate gaps, not one restated three ways — direction, possibility, and the efficiency limit are each their own mark.
